title: Factorization (1): Common Factors and Grouping
summary: Writing an expression as a product, taking out the highest common factor, and factorizing four-term expressions by grouping.

p: Factorization is writing an expression as a product of its factors. It is the opposite of expanding brackets. We factorize to simplify expressions, to solve equations, to find common factors and to cancel in fractions.

Take out the highest common factor (HCF) of all the terms. Example 1: 5x + 10 = 5(x + 2). Example 2: 3a – 9 = 3(a – 3). Example 3: 4x² + 8x = 4x(x + 2). Example 4: 6ab + 9a = 3a(2b + 3). Example 5: 12x³ – 18x² = 6x²(2x – 3). Example 6: 15xy – 10xz + 5x = 5x(3y – 2z + 1). Always check by expanding the answer.
For four terms, group them in pairs that share a factor, take out each common factor and then take out the common bracket.
Example 7: ax + ay + bx + by = a(x + y) + b(x + y) = (x + y)(a + b).
Example 8: 3m + 3p + mq + pq = 3(m + p) + q(m + p) = (m + p)(3 + q).
Example 9: 2x + 6y + ax + 3ay = 2(x + 3y) + a(x + 3y) = (x + 3y)(2 + a).

With minus signs, be careful. Example 11: ab – 2a + 3b – 6 = a(b – 2) + 3(b – 2) = (b – 2)(a + 3). Example 12: pq + 2p – 3q – 6 = p(q + 2) – 3(q + 2) = (q + 2)(p – 3). Example 13: ax – ay – bx + by = a(x – y) – b(x – y) = (x – y)(a – b). Grouping in a different order, (ax – bx) + (–ay + by) = x(a – b) – y(a – b) = (a – b)(x – y), gives the same answer.
Evaluation: 6x + 12 = 6(x + 2); ax + ay + bx + by = (x + y)(a + b); xy + 2x + 3y + 6 = (y + 2)(x + 3).

title: Factorization (2): Difference of Two Squares and Perfect Squares
summary: The identities a² – b² = (a + b)(a – b) and a² ± 2ab + b² = (a ± b)², with recognition tips and answers.

p: a² – b² = (a + b)(a – b). Look for two perfect squares with a minus sign between them.
With a common factor first: 2x² – 18 = 2(x² – 9) = 2(x + 3)(x – 3). 3a² – 75 = 3(a² – 25) = 3(a + 5)(a – 5).
x² + 4 cannot be factorized using real numbers, because there is no minus sign (a sum of two squares does not factorize).
a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)² and a² – 2ab + b² = (a – b)². How to recognise one: the first and last terms are perfect squares and the middle term is plus or minus twice the product of their square roots.

title: Factorization (3): Quadratic Trinomials and Applications
summary: Factorizing x² + bx + c by finding two numbers, then using factorization to find sides, simplify fractions and solve equations.

p: Find two numbers that multiply to give c and add to give b.

Example 28: x² + 7x + 12. Pairs that multiply to 12: 1 × 12 (sum 13), 2 × 6 (sum 8), 3 × 4 (sum 7). So (x + 3)(x + 4). Example 29: x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3). Example 30: x² – 5x + 6: the numbers must multiply to +6 and add to –5, so –2 and –3: (x – 2)(x – 3). Example 31: x² + 3x – 10: product –10, sum 3, so 5 and –2: (x + 5)(x – 2). Example 32: x² – 2x – 15: product –15, sum –2, so –5 and 3: (x – 5)(x + 3).
Sign tips: if c is positive, both numbers have the same sign as b. If c is negative, the numbers have different signs and the larger one has the sign of b.
Area: a rectangle has area x² + 7x + 12 and length (x + 4). Since x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4), the width is x + 3.
Numbers: x² + 3x + 2 = (x + 1)(x + 2), so the two consecutive numbers are x + 1 and x + 2.
Solving equations: if a product is zero, one of the factors is zero. x² – 5x + 6 = 0, so (x – 2)(x – 3) = 0, so x = 2 or x = 3. x² – 16 = 0, so (x + 4)(x – 4) = 0 and x = –4 or 4.

sections.h: Answers: Sections E, F and G
p: G: x² + 11x + 24 = (x + 3)(x + 8), so the width is x + 3. Simplify: (x² – 16)/(x + 4) = x – 4; (x² + 6x + 9)/(x + 3) = x + 3; (2x² – 8)/(x – 2) = 2(x + 2). Solve: x = ±3; (x + 2)(x + 5) = 0 gives x = –2 or –5; x = 2 or 3. The two consecutive odd numbers: x² + 4x + 3 = (x + 1)(x + 3). The square's side: 4x² + 12x + 9 = (2x + 3)², so the side is 2x + 3.
Evaluation: x² + 8x + 15 = (x + 3)(x + 5); (x² – 4)/(x + 2) = x – 2; x² – 7x + 12 = 0 gives (x – 3)(x – 4) = 0, so x = 3 or 4.

activity: Factorize x² + 9x + 20 ((x + 4)(x + 5)) and solve x² – x – 12 = 0 (x = 4 or –3).

title: Solving Simple Equations Involving Fractions
summary: How to clear fractions by multiplying by the LCM, with worked examples of one fraction, the same denominator and different denominators.

p: Multiply both sides by the denominator.

Example 1: x/3 = 5, so x = 15 (check: 15/3 = 5). Example 2: (x + 2)/4 = 3, so x + 2 = 12 and x = 10. Example 3: (2x – 1)/5 = 3, so 2x – 1 = 15, 2x = 16 and x = 8. Example 4: x/2 + 3 = 7, so x/2 = 4 and x = 8. Example 5: x/4 – 2 = 5, so x/4 = 7 and x = 28.
Example 6: x/3 + 2x/3 = 10, so 3x/3 = 10 and x = 10. Example 7: 3x/5 – x/5 = 4, so 2x/5 = 4, 2x = 20 and x = 10. Example 8: (x + 1)/4 + (x – 1)/4 = 3, so 2x/4 = 3 and x = 6.
Find the LCM of the denominators and multiply every term by it.
Example 9: x/2 + x/3 = 10. LCM 6: 3x + 2x = 60, so x = 12 (check: 6 + 4 = 10). Example 10: x/4 + x/6 = 5. LCM 12: 3x + 2x = 60, so x = 12. Example 11: x/3 – x/4 = 2. LCM 12: 4x – 3x = 24, so x = 24.

Example 12: (x + 1)/2 + (x – 1)/3 = 5. LCM 6: 3(x + 1) + 2(x – 1) = 30, so 5x + 1 = 30 and x = 29/5 = 5.8. Example 13: (2x + 3)/4 – (x – 2)/3 = 2. LCM 12: 3(2x + 3) – 4(x – 2) = 24, so 6x + 9 – 4x + 8 = 24, 2x = 7 and x = 3.5. Brackets: multiply every term, and take care with the minus sign in front of a bracket.

sections.h: Answers: Sections A, B and C
p: Evaluation: x/4 = 7 gives 28; (x + 3)/2 = 6 gives 9; x/2 + x/3 = 10 gives 12; x/5 – x/10 = 3 gives 30; (2x – 1)/3 = 5 gives 8; x/3 + 5 = 11 gives 18. The LCM of 4 and 6 is 12.

title: Fractional Equations with the Unknown in the Denominator
summary: Cross-multiplication, the rule that a denominator cannot be zero, and more complex fractional equations.

p: Warning: a denominator can never be zero, so a solution that makes it zero is not allowed. Division by zero has no meaning.

Example 14: 3/x = 6. Cross-multiply: 3 = 6x, so x = 1/2 (check: 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6). Example 15: 5/x + 2 = 7, so 5/x = 5 and x = 1. Example 16: 12/x = 4, so x = 3. Example 17: (x + 3)/x = 5, so x + 3 = 5x, 3 = 4x and x = 3/4. Example 18: 2/(x – 1) = 4, so 2 = 4x – 4, 6 = 4x and x = 1.5 (x is not 1, so it is allowed).

Example 21: 2/x + 3/(x + 1) = 1. Multiply by x(x + 1): 2(x + 1) + 3x = x(x + 1), so 5x + 2 = x² + x, giving x² – 4x – 2 = 0. This does not factorize, so we use the quadratic formula (which you will meet in SS1): x = (4 ± √24)/2 = 2 ± √6, so x ≈ 4.45 or x ≈ –0.45. Both values are allowed because neither makes a denominator zero.

D: 8/x = 4 gives x = 2; 12/x = 3 gives 4; 15/x = 5 gives 3; 6/x + 2 = 8 gives x = 1; 10/x – 3 = 2 gives x = 2; (x + 4)/x = 3 gives x = 2; (2x – 3)/x = 5 gives –3 = 3x so x = –1; 3/(x – 1) = 6 gives x = 1.5; 4/(x + 2) = 2 gives x = 0; 5/(2x – 1) = 5 gives 2x – 1 = 1 so x = 1.
Evaluation: 6/x = 3 gives x = 2. The denominator cannot be zero because division by zero is not defined.

title: Word Problems Leading to Fractional Equations
summary: Number, age, speed, pipe-filling and work-rate problems solved with fractional equations, with answers to the practice questions.

p: Example 22: one-third of a number plus 5 is 17. x/3 + 5 = 17, so x/3 = 12 and x = 36. Example 23: half a number minus 8 equals one-quarter of it: x/2 – 8 = x/4. Multiply by 4: 2x – 32 = x, so x = 32. Example 24: two-thirds of a number plus one-quarter of it is 22: 2x/3 + x/4 = 22, so 8x + 3x = 264 and x = 24.
If a job takes t hours, the rate is 1/t of the job per hour. Add the rates when workers or pipes work together; subtract when one pipe empties.
Example 25: pipe 1 fills 1/4 of a tank per hour and pipe 2 fills 1/6. Together 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12 per hour, so the time is 12/5 = 2.4 hours = 2 hours 24 minutes.
Example 26: Peter paints a room in 3 hours and Paul in 6 hours. Together 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2 per hour, so 2 hours.
Example 30: an inlet fills a cistern in 5 hours and an outlet empties it in 8 hours. Net rate 1/5 – 1/8 = 3/40 per hour, so the time is 40/3 = 13⅓ hours.

Example 27: a fraction becomes 1/2 when 1 is added to numerator and denominator, and 1/3 when 1 is subtracted from both. Let the fraction be x/y. (x + 1)/(y + 1) = 1/2 gives y = 2x + 1. (x – 1)/(y – 1) = 1/3 gives y = 3x – 2. So 2x + 1 = 3x – 2, x = 3 and y = 7. The fraction is 3/7. Check: 4/8 = 1/2 and 2/6 = 1/3.
Example 28: a trip takes 4 hours at 60 km/h. The distance is 240 km. If the time is reduced by one-third, the new time is 4 – 4/3 = 8/3 hours and the new speed is 240 ÷ 8/3 = 90 km/h.
Example 29: A's age is 2/3 of B's and the sum is 45. x + 2x/3 = 45, so 5x = 135, B = 27 and A = 18.

activity: Taps A and B fill a bath in 6 and 12 hours respectively; how long together (4 hours)? One-fifth of a number plus 8 is 12. Find it (20).

title: Change of Subject of a Formula (1): Basic Types
summary: What a formula and its subject are, why we change the subject, and the inverse-operation rules, with examples involving addition, multiplication and powers.

p: A formula is an equation that shows the relationship between variables. Examples: A = lb (area of a rectangle), P = 2(l + b), v = d/t and I = PRT/100. The subject is the variable on its own on one side (usually the left). In v = d/t, v is the subject.
We change the subject to find a different quantity: from v = d/t, d = vt gives distance, and t = d/v gives time.

1. Do the same thing to both sides. 2. Use inverse operations: addition and subtraction, multiplication and division, squaring and square root, cubing and cube root. 3. Isolate the wanted variable. 4. Keep the equation balanced.

Example 1: a = b + c gives b = a – c. Example 2: q = p – r gives p = q + r. Example 3: y + x = z gives x = z – y. Example 4: P = 2(l + h): divide by 2 to get P/2 = l + h, then h = P/2 – l = (P – 2l)/2. Example 5: s = p + q + r gives r = s – p – q.

Example 6: v = πr²h gives r² = v/(πh), so r = √[v/(πh)]. Example 7: v = d/t gives t = d/v. Example 8: I = PRT/100: 100I = PRT, so P = 100I/(RT). Example 9: A = bh/2: 2A = bh, so b = 2A/h. Example 10: E = mc² gives m = E/c².

Example 11: A = πr² gives r = √(A/π). Example 12: v = √(2gh): square both sides to get v² = 2gh, so h = v²/(2g). Example 13: T = 2π√(l/g): divide by 2π, square both sides, T²/(4π²) = l/g, so l = gT²/(4π²). Example 14: c² = a² + b² gives a = √(c² – b²). Example 15: y² = 4x gives x = y²/4.
A: x = y – 5; q = p + r; n = t – m; c = a – b – d; x = z + y; u = s – at; l = (P – 2w)/2; x = (y – c)/m; b = A – c; y = (10 – x)/2.
B: b = A/l; t = d/v; h = V/(lw); r = C/(2π); a = F/m; P = 100I/(RT); a = (v – u)/t; m = E/c²; h = 2A/b; h = P/(ρg).
Evaluation: b = a – c; t = d/s; r = √(A/π); h = V/(lw). The inverse of addition is subtraction; the inverse of squaring is the square root.

activity: Make t the subject of s = vt (t = s/v). Make r the subject of A = 4πr² (r = √(A/4π)).

title: Change of Subject (2): Combined Operations and Real Formulas
summary: Formulas that need several steps, a method of working backwards, and practical formulas from science and geometry, with answers.

p: Example 16: y = 3x + 5 gives y – 5 = 3x, so x = (y – 5)/3. Example 18: A = P(1 + r)ⁿ: A/P = (1 + r)ⁿ, then take the nth root to get 1 + r = (A/P)^(1/n), so r = (A/P)^(1/n) – 1. Example 19: a = (b + c)/2 gives 2a = b + c, so b = 2a – c. Example 20: x = √(y + 3) gives x² = y + 3, so y = x² – 3.
1. Identify the variable to make the subject. 2. List the operations done to it. 3. Undo them with inverse operations, in reverse order. 4. Simplify.
Example 26: y = 2(x + 3) – 5. On x: add 3, multiply by 2, subtract 5. Undo in reverse: y + 5 = 2(x + 3); (y + 5)/2 = x + 3; x = (y + 5)/2 – 3 = (y – 1)/2.

Temperature: F = (9/5)C + 32 gives C = (5/9)(F – 32). Motion: v = u + at gives a = (v – u)/t. Ohm's law: V = IR gives R = V/I. Kinetic energy: KE = ½mv² gives v = √(2KE/m). Circumference: C = 2πr gives r = C/(2π). Trapezium: A = ½(a + b)h gives a = 2A/h – b. Cone: V = ⅓πr²h gives h = 3V/(πr²). Compound interest: A = P(1 + r)ⁿ gives P = A/(1 + r)ⁿ. Resistance: R = ρl/A gives A = ρl/R.

sections.h: Answers: Sections C, D, E and F
p: E: T = 100I/(PR); d = C/π; s = vt; M = DV; F = PA; h = V/(πr²); a = 2A/h – b; m = 2KE/v²; I = V/R; P = A/(1 + r)ⁿ.

F: x = (y – 1)/2; r = ∛(3V/(4π)); for s = ut + ½at² the unknown t appears twice, so you need the quadratic formula: t = [–u + √(u² + 2as)]/a (this is a challenge question beyond JSS 3); from √(x + y) = z, x = z² – y; from 1/a + 1/b = 1/c, 1/b = 1/c – 1/a = (a – c)/(ac), so b = ac/(a – c).

title: First Term Revision: Whole Numbers, Binary, Numbers, Variation and Algebra
summary: A checklist, key formulas and exam tips for the whole first term, with notes on the corrections made.

p: Binary numbers: conversion, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division. Words into algebra: expressions and equations. BODMAS, brackets and fractions. Direct and inverse proportion. Compound interest and depreciation. Rational and irrational numbers. Variation: direct, inverse, joint, partial, combined. Factorization: common factors, grouping, difference of two squares, perfect squares, trinomials. Fractional equations. Change of subject.
A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ; y = kx; y = k/x; z = kxy; y = kx + c; a² – b² = (a + b)(a – b); a² ± 2ab + b² = (a ± b)²; x² + bx + c = (x + p)(x + q) with pq = c and p + q = b.

The binary total 10110₂ + 1101₂ + 1010₂ is 101101₂, not 101011₂. The 'workers' example moved from direct to inverse proportion. √(–4) is not a real number. The step-by-step division of 10101₂ ÷ 11₂ and 1001₂ ÷ 11₂ was completed. 22/7 and 3.14 are approximations of π, not equal to it.

Always check binary answers by changing to decimal. In variation questions find k first. In factorizing, take out the common factor first and check by expanding. For fractional equations, find the LCM, multiply every term and check that no denominator is zero. Show your working.

activity: Do a mixed past paper in 90 minutes. List the three topics you found hardest and work three more questions on each.
